title: False Daisy (Higis Manok): How to Spot and Control It in Rice
metaTitle: False Daisy in Rice: Spot and Control Higis Manok
metaDescription: False daisy, or higis manok, has reddish stems that root at the joints in lowland rice. Learn to spot it and stop it before its white flowers seed.
excerpt: False daisy is a broadleaf weed that many Filipino farmers call higis manok. It has reddish stems, and when it blooms, it shows small white flower heads. You can find it in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields across the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it among your palay and how it competes with your crop. It also shows how to control it before it seeds.

blocks.text:
False daisy is a small annual damo from the sunflower family, Asteraceae. Its scientific name is Eclipta prostrata. Farmers know it as higis manok, tultulisan or tinta tinta. It has soft, fleshy stems and leaves set in pairs. Its tiny white flower heads look like a little daisy, and that is why people gave it its English name.

You can find it in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields. This weed completes its life in one season. Within a single crop it sprouts, flowers, sets seed and dies. It spreads by seed, and each flower head makes many small seeds. Its stems also put out roots wherever they touch moist soil. So a plant that leans over can anchor itself in more places and keep growing.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about false daisy
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Check for a low plant with soft, reddish, hairy stems. When a stem touches wet soil, look for small roots at the joints. The leaves are dark green and grow in pairs, one opposite the other. They are long and narrow, and if you look closely, the edges show clear teeth. Like other broadleaf weeds, the leaves have netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. Then look for small white flower heads, about 1 cm across, at the stem tips and leaf joints.

items: Reddish, fleshy stems covered with short hairs, lying low or standing among the rice.
Small roots growing from the stem joints wherever the stem touches wet soil.
Dark green, narrow leaves set in opposite pairs along the stem.
Leaf edges with clear, small teeth that you can see up close.
White flower heads about 1 cm across, made of many tiny white florets.
Look alike tip: Eclipta zippeliana has light green, much hairier leaves with coarse, spiny teeth.

blocks.text:
Higis manok competes with your palay for light, water and fertilizer. It grows well on wet soil, so it fits right into a lowland rice field. Young rice is hit hardest, because it is still small when the weed fills the spaces between hills. Every handful of fertilizer the weed takes is food your crop does not get.

Because it is an annual that spreads by seed, each plant that flowers adds more seeds to your soil. That is why the same patch comes back crop after crop. Its seeds can also mix with harvested palay and lower its quality. Thick weedy spots can give insects and rats a place to hide as well.

items: Hand weed early, while the plants are small. Pull the whole plant, including any rooted stem joints, and carry it out of the paddy.
Do not leave pulled plants lying on wet soil. The stems can root again at the joints and keep growing.
Remove plants before the white flower heads mature. Each head holds many small seeds that will sprout again next season.
Clean the bunds and canal edges too. Plants growing there can drop seed back into the field.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold false daisy down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep False Daisy Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is False Daisy?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About False Daisy

items.q: What is false daisy called in Tagalog and other local names?
items.a: Farmers know it by several names. Many call it higis manok, tultulisan or tinta tinta. In English it is false daisy, and its scientific name is Eclipta prostrata. A close cousin, Eclipta zippeliana, shares the same local names. So if you need to tell them apart, check the leaf color and the hairs.

items.q: How do I get rid of higis manok in my rice field?
items.a: Start with good land preparation and clean seed, then keep proper water in the paddy. Hand weed early and pull out the whole plant with its rooted joints. If you need a herbicide, choose one for broadleaf weeds that matches the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label on the product.

items.q: Why does higis manok keep coming back every season?
items.a: It is an annual, but each plant makes many seeds. If even a few plants flower, they refill the soil with seed for the next crop. Its stems can also root at the joints, so pieces left on wet soil may keep growing. Pull it early, before it flowers, and do it every season to bring the seed supply down.
